584; I replaced the hutsville tester codes with the Source code version ID so that I can always see what version of the codebase
585; the cal is based on. This may be similar functionality to the original, though I don't know the meaning of the Huntsville codes.
586;
587; Codes:
588;
589; The first byte is the codebase type (LM, SMEC, SBEC, etc.)
590;
591; a = T-LM
592; b = T-SMEC
593; c = T-SBEC
594; d = T-TIII (91)
595; e = T-TIII (92-93)
596; f = ??
597;
598; The 2nd byte is the source code version in HEX. For example:
599; 0x10 = 16dec = version 16
600 
601; ***********************************************************************
602;
603; ***********************************************************************
604;
605; *** Config/Option Constants ***
606;
607; These constants alow the user to enable/disable all of the
608; added special functions without having to re-assemble from the source.
609; These bits can be set/cleared in CHeM or D-Cal.
610;
611; ***********************************************************************
612;
613; *** Spark/Fuel Rev Limiters ***
614;
615; You can now enable/dis-able independantly the spark/fuel rev limiters.
616; The Spark-based rev limiter is new. The stock code onyl cut fuel for
617; the rev limiter (and overboost, speed limiter, etc.). This was a little
618; rough when used for the 2-step. So, I added an option to use a spark
619; limiter as well as -or in addition to- the fuel-based rev limiter.
620;
621; *** Switchable boost ***
622;
623; Switchable boost uses an additional boost from RPM table to limit the
624; boost when the switch is inactive. Depending on the switch used, it may
625; be active high or active low. The polarity flag is there to allow the
626; user to set the switch to function as intended regardless of the switch
627; used.
628;
629; *** Staging Limiter/2-Step ***
630;
631; The staging limiter has 2 activation/deactivation methods.
632; 1st, the limiter checks to see if it's active by looking for an "enable"
633; switch. This could be the brake or other input switch.
634; If the switch is "off", then the normal rev limiter values are used.
635; 2nd, the limiter checks to see if the vehicle speed is below the cutoff
636; point - STGSPD. If it is, then the normal rev limiter value is loaded.
637;
638; !!! RPM is used differently in the '89 T1 code than the previous codebases.
639; !!! Actual RPM is used, rather than the time between dist pulses (used in the
640; !!! LM and T2 SMEC codebases).
641;
642; *** Flash CE on Knock ***
643;
644; This option allows the user to flash the "Check Engine" lamp when knock is
645; indicated. The individual cylinder retards are used for knock detection.
646; In use, the lamp will flash proportionately to the amount of knock.
647; It is also possible to use the PTU/Upshift indicator as a knock light (this
648; ouput is not used on turbo cars). I may add that as an option in the future.
649;
650; *** Hi-Speed logger ***
651;
652; The hi-speed logger allows for much faster than stock datalogging rates
653; using an external logging program. It also disables all DRB routines, so
654; communication with a standard scantool will no longer be possible. The
655; option flag allows the feature to be turned on/off without losing
656; calibration data. the function is very simple in operation. It loads a
657; single byte memory address into B and then send the data stored at that
658; address to the serial port.
659;
660; *** Anti-lag ***
661;
662; See description at the anti-lag routine for the specifics.
663;
664; ***********************************************************************
665 
666 ;.org 0x800c

749; ***********************************************************************
750; ERROR CODE MASKS
751; ***********************************************************************
752; Error code "masking" is implemented differently in the '89 T1 than in the earlier code.
753; Instead of masking bits for the individual codes, an internal code is used to mask up to
754; 7 different code bytes. The code bytes are as follows:
755;
756; Code # Code Offset (masking code)
757; 61 Baro sensor open or shorted 31
758; 62 EMR mileage cannot be stored in EEPROM 30
759; 63 Controller cannot write to EEPROM 2f
760;
761; 44 Loss of FJ2 08,2c
762; 45 Nothing (overboost) 07
763; 46 Battery Volts High 06
764; 47 Battery Volts Low 05
765; 51 Lean condition 04
766; 52 Rich Condition 03,2d
767; 53 Prom Checksum 02
768; 54 Distributor Sync 01
769;
770; 33 AC Cutout Relay 10
771; 34 Speed Ctl Solenoid 0f
772; 35 Radiator Fan Relay 0e
773; 36 Wastegate Solenoid 0d
774; 37 Barometric Read Solenoid 0c
775; 41 Charging System 0b
776; 42 Auto Shutdown Relay 0a
777; 43 Ignition Coil Control 09,28,29,2b
778;
779; 22 Coolant Temp Sensor 1e,1f
780; 23 Charge Temp Sensor 1c,1d
781; 24 Throttle Position 1a,1b
782; 25 AIS Motor 19
783; 26 Injector Current Limit Not Achieved 16,17,18
784; 27 Injector Driver interface 13,14,15
785; 31 Purge Solenoid 12
786; 32 Exh Gas Recirc Solenoid 11,2e
787;
788; 11 Engine Not Cranked Since Battery Disconnected 28
789; 12 Memory Standby Power Lost 00
790; 13 MAP Pneumatic 26,27
791; 14 MAP Electrical 24,25
792; 15 Vehicle Distance Sensor 23
793; 16 Battery Voltage Sense 22
794; 17 Engine Running Too Cool (thermostat) 21
795; 21 Oxygen Sensor 20
796;
797; The "internal" or "masking" code is actually the offset used to lookup the code
798; in the table 'ErrorCodesToDash_Table'
799;
800; The last byte MUST be 0x00, otherwise the code will result in an error.
801; I think the original intent was to allow the factory calibrators to mask
802; specific internal codes to try and debug errors. Previously, only the final
803; error code could be masked - making the cause unclear in the case where multiple
804; internal codes set the same error code.
805;
806; It should be possible to increase the size of the list by adding additional code
807; bytes after "FLTMSK7_ErrorBitsMask7". Just make sure that the byte after the last one in
808; the list remains 0x00. The mask cheking routine looks for this to mark the end of
809; the list. Also, if the list is too long, it may cause lack of space for other
810; items. So, be careful if adding to this list.
811

1993; *****************************************************************************
1994; Cold Enrichment Factor Calculation (CNRICH)
1995;
1996; 1 + ((CURVEA * ACVDCY/256 + CURVEC * ACVDCY/256 + CURVEB * FCRCVB/256) * 2 +
1997; (HMPMUL * HIGHMP)/32) * BAROCP/256
1998;
1999; CURVEA, CURVEB, CURVEC Factors:
2000; X == Engine Temp DegC + 128 ( Engine Temp is scaled between -128C and +128C
2001; -198F and +262F
2002; Y == (Factor - 1) * 128 where the factor is between 1.00 and 2.99
2003;
2004; *****************************************************************************
2005

2159; *****************************************************************************
2160; Load Enrichment:
2161; Cold Load Factor == HIGHMP * HMPMUL/32
2162;
2163; HIGHMP Factors:
2164; X - Engine Temp
2165; Y - (% enrichment per Torr/100) * 32 * 5.88 * 256

3195; *****************************************
3196; O2 Controller Ramp Calibration
3197; *****************************************
3198; How it works:
3199; The O2 sensor is monitored but ONLY for "rich/lean". Even though
3200; the O2 sensor value is from 0 to 15, the only thing that counts
3201; for this system is whether it is "rich" or "lean". A change from one
3202; to the other is a "toggle". The system constantly toggles between
3203; rich and lean so that the overall average is around stoichiometric.
3204;
3205; Background information (from the net:)
3206; An "ideal" fuel/air mixture in which both the fuel and the oxygen in the air are
3207; completely consumed is called the "stoichiometric" mixture. The stoichiometric mixture
3208; is usually specified as the ratio of the mass of air to the mass of a particular fuel.
3209; For example, if a fuel required 10 kg of air to precisely burn 1 kg of the fuel (that is,
3210; all the fuel burned and there was no oxygen left in the air afterwards) then the
3211; stoichiometric ratio for that fuel would be 10:1.
3212;
3213; Chevron give the stoichiometric ratio of air mass to fuel mass for gasoline as 14.7:1,
3214; but don't specify the composition of this hypothetical gasoline.
3215;
3216; From http://www.faqs;.org/faqs/autos/gasoline-faq/part2/ comes the following table
3217; of typical stoichiometric air-fuel ratios:
3218;
3219; Fuel | Stoichiometric air-fuel ratio
3220; -----------+------------------------------
3221; methanol | 6.4
3222; ethanol | 9.0
3223; MTBE | 11.7
3224; ETBE, TAME | 12.1
3225; gasoline | 14.6
3226;
3227; An oxygenated gasoline with 89% gasoline and 11% MTBE would then have a stoichiometric
3228; ratio of 14.281 (note that this would require a Wide Band O2 sensor to adjust, since the
3229; O2 sensor in our cars is designed for gasoline only, and is a very narrow range. In case
3230; you were wondering, this is one reason some people are interested in Wide Band O2 sensors.)
3231;
3232; *****************************************
3233; This system divides a range of RPMs and MAP readings into "cells". The number of
3234; "kicks", or increases/decreases in fuel required to toggle the O2 reading, is different
3235; for each of these cells. This allows some fairly powerful flexibility in tuning. The
3236; only time you might want to adjust these values is for different injector flow rates,
3237; or to speed or slow the adjustment being performed.
3238; *****************************************
3239; Note to tuners: DO NOT AIM FOR STOICHIOMETRY! Although it might be fine for idle or
3240; low speed operation, at higher RPMs and under boost you DEFINITELY want a RICH mixture.
3241; This is because stoichiometric combustion generates the most heat. No current engine
3242; would survive very long with the temperatures this would generate, hot enough to melt
3243; the engine.
3244; *****************************************
3245; Each cell has a kick value. This is the amount of change applied to the running fuel
3246; every eleven millisec until a rich/lean toggle occurs. The net result is the
3247; familiar rich/lean flashing that your O2 sensor gauge shows you.
3248; *****************************************
3249;
3250; (one kick per 11ms)
3251; Fudge factor: if an O2 toggle occurs before the primary ramp
3252; finishes, then the "first" step in the new direction is limited
3253; to the accumulated steps before the toggle.
3254;
3255; Cells:
3256;
3257; HIRPM +-----+-----+-----+
3258; | 2 | 5 | 8 |
3259; RPM#2 +-----+-----+-----+
3260; | 1 | 4 | 7 |
3261; RPM#1 +-----+-----+-----+
3262; | 0 | 3 | 6 | Idle Cell: 9
3263; +-----+-----+-----+
3264; Map#1 MAP#2 HIMAP
3265;
3266; *****************************************
3267; PrimaryO2Ramp:
3268; *****************************************
3269

7633; I changed the MAP transfer function constants to be read from a constant value, rather than hard-coded
7634; into the binary. This makes it easier to find/change these values when changing MAP sensors.
7635;
7636; I'll add more info about the MAP transfer function later, but basically these constants are only used
7637; to convert MAP volts to MAP pressure. NOT for altering 2 to 3- bar. These constants will be unique for
7638; each MAP sensor (but should be the same for a given type/manufacturer).
